Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 91, verse 1–15:

(p-627) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surah ash-Shams (The Sun)

It is Meccan.

The Exalted and Majestic One said:

﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ ﴿and the moon when it follows it﴾ ﴿and the day when it displays it﴾ ﴿and the night when it covers it﴾ ﴿and the heaven and He who built it﴾ ﴿and the earth and He who spread it out﴾ ﴿and the soul and He who proportioned it﴾ ﴿and inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness﴾ ﴿He has certainly succeeded who purifies it﴾ ﴿and he has certainly failed who corrupts it﴾ ﴿Thamud denied in their transgression﴾ ﴿when the most wretched of them was sent forth﴾ ﴿and the Messenger of Allah said to them: "The she-camel of Allah, and her drinking"﴾ ﴿but they denied him and hamstrung her, so their Lord crushed them over their sin and leveled them﴾ ﴿and He does not fear its consequence﴾

Allah the Exalted swears by the sun, either as a reminder through it, or as an assumed oath "and the Lord of the sun." "Ad-duha" with a damma on the dad and with the alif maqsura means the rising and completion of light. Mujahid explained it this way. Qatadah said: it is the entire day. Muqatil said:

"Duhaha" (its brightness): its heat, as in His saying, the Exalted, in Ta-Ha ﴿nor will you be exposed to the sun's heat﴾ [Ta-Ha: 119]. "Ad-duha" with a fatha on the dad and with the mad: what lies above that until midday.

The moon follows the sun from the beginning of the month until its middle at sunset: the sun sets, then the moon sets; and it follows it in the second half in another manner, which is that the sun sets and then the moon rises. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: "talaha" means it follows it constantly at every time; because it receives light from it, so it follows it for that reason.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is following that is not specific to the first half or the last half of the month. Al-Farra' also said this. Az-Zajjaj and others said: "talaha" means it becomes full and round, so it is a follower of it in rank of light and measure (p-628), because among the stars there is nothing that follows the sun in this sense except the moon. Qatadah said: that is only on the night of the full moon, when the sun sets and the moon rises.

"An-nahar" in the apparent sense of this surah and the one after it is that it begins from the sunrise, and az-Zajjaj said likewise in Kitab al-Anwa' and elsewhere. The day begins from the dawn, and there is no disagreement that the end of both is the setting of the sun. The pronoun in ﴿jallaha﴾ may refer to the sun, and may refer to the earth and to the darkness, although there has been no mention of that, the meaning requires it, as az-Zajjaj said. Jalla means it revealed and illuminated, and the subject of "jalla," according to these interpretations, is the day. It is also possible that the subject is Allah the Exalted, as if He said: "and the day when Allah displays the sun," so He swears by the day in its most complete state. "Yaghsha" means it covers, and the pronoun refers to the sun by a figurative usage, or to the earth.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and He who built it﴾, and everything after it of its like in the surah: "ma" in it may be in the sense of "alladhi" (who). Abu 'Ubayda said: that is, "and He who built it," and this is the view of al-Hasan and Mujahid, because "ma" generally applies to those who have reason and to those who do not, so the oath is by Himself, the Exalted. It is also possible that "ma" in all of that is a verbal noun (masdariyya), said by Qatadah, al-Mubarrad, and az-Zajjaj, as if He, the Exalted, said: "and the heaven and its construction."

"Tahaa" means "daha" (spread out). "Tahaa" in the language also means: to go every way, and from it is the saying of 'Alqama ibn 'Abada:

Your heart has been drawn away by the beautiful women, a heart that is easily moved, far from youth, its age has come to grey hair.

"An-nafs" by which He swore is a generic noun. Its "proportioning" is the completion of its intellect and its reasoning, and for this reason He linked the speech with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿then He inspired it with its wickedness﴾... the verse. The fa' indicates that the proportioning is this inspiration. The meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿then He inspired it with its wickedness﴾ is: its knowledge of that is what guides it, and He made for it (p-629) a power with which the acquisition of wickedness and the acquisition of righteousness are possible.

The answer to the oath is in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He has certainly succeeded﴾, and the implied meaning is: "Indeed, he has succeeded." The subject of "zakka" may be Allah the Exalted, and this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and others, as if He, the Exalted, said: "The group or the party that Allah the Exalted has purified has certainly succeeded." "Man" applies to plural and singular. The subject of "zakka" may be the human being, and "man" refers to him; this was said by al-Hasan and others, as if He, the Exalted, said: "He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself," that is, who acquires the purity that Allah the Exalted created for him. "Zakkaha" means: He purified it and made it grow with good deeds. "Dassaha" means: He concealed it and degraded it, that is, he belittled its worth by sins and by stinginess with what is obligatory. It is said: "dasa yadsu," and "dassa" with a doubled sin, "yudassi," and its root is "dassa," and from it is the saying of the poet:

I buried 'Amr in the dust, and his wives have become weak, weeping for the loss.

It is related that the Prophet ﷺ, when he recited this verse, would say: "O Allah, grant my soul its piety, and purify it, You are the best of those who purify it, You are its Guardian and its Master." This hadith strengthens the view that the one who purifies is Allah the Exalted. Tha'lab said: the meaning of the verse is: "And he has certainly failed who corrupts it" among the people of good by hypocrisy, while he is not among them in reality.

When the Exalted mentioned the description of him who corrupts, He mentioned a group who did that so that one may take heed from them and refrain from the likes of their deed. "At-Taghwa" is a verbal noun. Al-Hasan and Hammad ibn Sulayman read "bitaghwaha" with a damma on the ta', a verbal noun like "al-'uqba" and "ar-ruj'a." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "At-taghwa" here is the punishment, (p-630) that they denied it until it descended upon them. This interpretation is supported by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿As for Thamud, they were destroyed by the overwhelming blast﴾ [al-Haqqa: 5]. The majority of interpreters said the "ba'" is causal, and the meaning is: Thamud denied their prophet because of their transgression and disbelief. "Inba'atha" is an expression for his going forth to the camel's hamstringing with vigor and eagerness. "Ashqaha" is Qidar ibn Salif, one of the nine corrupt men. It is possible that "ashqaha" applies to a group who attempted the hamstringing. It is related that he did not do his deed to the camel until the whole tribe supported him in that; for this reason He said, the Exalted: ﴿so they hamstrung her﴾, because they were all agreed upon it.

"Rasul Allah" is Salih, peace be upon him. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿the she-camel of Allah and her drinking﴾ is in the accusative by a hidden verb whose estimate is: "Guard," or "Leave," or "Beware," in the sense of: "Beware of neglecting her right." The matter of the she-camel and the drinking has already been mentioned in other than this surah, so it suffices without repetition. He, the Exalted, put the denial before the hamstringing because it was the cause of the hamstringing. It is related that they had embraced Islam before that and followed Salih, peace be upon him, for a period, then they denied and stumbled. Most of the exegetes hold that they remained on their disbelief. "Damdama" means: He sent down punishment upon them, disturbing them, repeating it; this is "ad-damdama." In some copies of the Qur'an it is "fa-dahdama," which is the reading of Ibn az-Zubayr with a ha' between the two dals; in some it is "fa-dammara," and in the Mushaf of Ibn Mas'ud it is "fa-damdamaha 'alayhim." His saying, the Exalted: "bidhanbihim," that is, because of their sin. His saying, the Exalted: "fasawwaha," means: He leveled the tribe in destruction; not one of them was spared.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-A'raj, the people of the Hijaz, and Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "fa-la yakhafu" with a fa', and likewise in the copies of the people of Madina and Syria. The rest read "wa-la yakhafu" with a waw, and likewise in their copies. It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he recited: "wa-lam yakhaf 'uqbaha." The subject of "yakhafu" according to the one who reads "fa-la yakhafu" with a fa' may be Allah the Exalted, and the meaning is: there is no pursuit against Allah the Exalted in His action toward them; He is not questioned about what He does. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan, and in this meaning is contempt for the people and the effacing of their trace. It is also possible that it is Salih, peace be upon him, meaning he does not fear the consequence of Allah for this deed against them, since he had warned them and cautioned them. (p-631) Whoever reads "wa-la yakhafu" with a waw, the two possibilities we mentioned are possible for it. It is also possible, in addition, that the subject of "yakhafu" is "ashqaha," the one who rushed forth. This was said by az-Zajjaj and Abu 'Ali, and it is the view of as-Suddi, ad-Dahhak, and Muqatil, and the waw is the waw of circumstance, as if He, the Exalted, said: "He rushed forth for her hamstringing, while he does not fear the consequence of his deed because of his disbelief and transgression." "Al-'Uqba" is the recompense of a thing, its end, and what comes after things as their consequence.

The reciters differed regarding the alifs of this surah and the two following it. Ibn Kathir and 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read them with fatha. al-Kisa'i read all of that with imala (inclination). Nafi' read all of them between fatha and imala. Hamza read "wa-duha" with kasra, and "talaha" and "tahaha" with fatha, and read the rest with kasra. Narrations from Abu 'Amr differ: at one time he read all of them with kasra, and at another time like the reading of Nafi'. Az-Zajjaj said: people call imala "kasr," and it is not a correct kasr. Al-Khalil and Abu 'Amr say: it is imala.

The tafsir of Surat ash-Shams is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
